newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD must emulate Britain's Labour - Schroeder.
newsitem.headline: German SPD must emulate Britain's Labour - Schroeder.

text.p: Germany's Gerhard Schroeder, a potential opposition Social Democrat (SPD) candidate for Chancellor, on Saturday said the SPD needed to follow the example of Britain's victorious Labour party and reform.
"The SPD wants to win, therefore it will understand that we have to change ourselves," Schroeder told Focus news magazine in an interview released ahead of publication on Monday.
"Otherwise the danger is too great that we will be written off as old-fashioned," he said.

Some commentators say Schroeder, the media-friendly and pro-business premier of Lower Saxony state, is the closest thing Germany has to Britain's Tony Blair, who led his newly-modernised Labour party to election victory on Friday.
"Against the background of Blair's success we must solve the open questions of our programme in the SPD," he said.

Schroeder called on his party to reach out to those it had once labelled as the better-off and redefine its relationship to modern technology. "For years we have only discussed the risks of technical advance and not the chances," he said.
But commentators say, in contrast to Blair, Schroeder is an outsider in the SPD and could only run against Chancellor Helmut Kohl with the agreement of SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine.
Lafontaine is seen as closer to the left and his party's favourite to challenge Kohl, despite losing to him in the 1990 general elections.
But opinion polls say Schroeder, currently on a tour of the United States to meet business leaders, has a far better chance of ousting Kohl, who has been in power since 1982.
Schroeder said economic globalisation was driving the need for reform in Germany and said the country had to consider how much of the welfare state was still financially viable.
"That does not mean the abolition of the welfare state, rather its new definition," he said.
Schroeder said the faster the economy changed, the faster one had to define what the state could afford. "This will hurt many of us, but the SPD must also carry out this process."
SPD party manager Franz Muentefering told Cologne's Express Sunday edition the party would stick to its plans to nominate its chancellor candidate at its congress in April next year.
Muentefering said the SPD would not make the same mistake as Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU) of announcing their candidate too early.
"The union (CDU/CSU) is doubting whether it has the right candidate. It will be a difficult year and a half for candidate Kohl and the union," he said.
Kohl announced last month he would stand for a fifth term in general elections due late next year.
